label: Irreversibility of morphogenesis, not Weismann's barrier, is what limits Lamarckism
claim: Because morphogenesis is a recursive, highly emergent process, the inverse problem of determining which genomic changes would produce a desired large-scale anatomical feature is in general unsolvable, and this irreversibility, rather than any inability to edit the germline in light of somatic experience, is what limits full-scale Lamarckian inheritance.
quote: This irreversibility of the recursive, highly emergent process of morphogenesis is what limits full-scale Lamarckism: the difficulty is not how to penetrate Weismann’s barrier and edit the genome in light of somatic experience—mechanisms exist for this [21–23].
scope: Metazoan development and inheritance in general
candidate_data: none known

label: Evolution searches the space of behaviour-shaping signals rather than local rules
claim: Because metazoan cells are agential (they retain adaptive behaviours from unicellular ancestors), what evolution mainly searches is not the enormous space of all possible local rules but the space of behaviour-shaping signals by which cells hack each other's functionality, and the collective intelligence of cell swarms strongly affects the rate and course of evolution.
quote: I argue that what evolution is really searching is not the enormous space of all possible local rules, but instead the space of behavior-shaping signals by which cells hack each other’s functionality, and that the collective intelligence [38, 39] of cellular swarms has major implications for the rate and course of evolution.
scope: Evolution of metazoan anatomy
measurable_quantities: rate of evolutionary improvement in models with vs without competent cells
edit distance between fit genotypes under bottom-up vs behaviour-shaping search
candidate_data: Evolutionary simulations of developmental systems with and without cellular competency; comparative evo-devo datasets.

label: A generative, compressed genome pushes evolution toward general-purpose problem solvers
claim: By using an architecture akin to a variational autoencoder, in which the genome is a compressed generative representation decoded by the developmental layer, evolution is kept from over-training on past conditions and is pushed to produce general-purpose problem-solving organisms that display robustness, plasticity and adaptive success in entirely novel circumstances.
quote: Second is that by using a variational autoencoder-like architecture of compression into a generative genome (Fig. 1), evolution is freed from over-training on past conditions and pushed to evolve general-purpose problem-solving machines which inevitably display robustness, plasticity, and adaptive success in entirely novel circumstances.
scope: Evolution of multicellular organisms
measurable_quantities: performance of evolved developmental models on novel perturbations
robustness of organisms to evolutionarily novel stressors
candidate_data: Evolutionary-computation experiments with generative genotype–phenotype maps; experimental data on responses of organisms to evolutionarily novel perturbations.

label: Gap-junction coupling scales cell competencies into larger collective goal states
claim: Basal cellular competencies were not lost in the transition to multicellularity but scaled up into collective intelligence; gap-junctional merging of intracellular milieus and other tissue-level signalling (e.g. stress propagation) share chemical engrams, erase the individuality of cells, and enlarge the memory, predictive capacity and sensory/effector radius of cell networks so they can pursue larger goal states such as anatomical targets.
quote: This promotes sharing of chemical engrams, which also help to wipe the individuality of cells, and enlarges the memory, predictive capacity, and sensory/effector radius of cellular networks, enabling them to pursue larger goal states in spaces like anatomical morphospace [14].
scope: Multicellular tissues coupled by gap junctions
measurable_quantities: gap-junctional coupling strength
spatial extent of coordinated cell responses
persistence of tissue-level memory
candidate_data: Gap-junction (connexin/innexin) perturbation studies, dye-coupling and calcium-wave imaging data in public image repositories such as the Image Data Resource.

label: Freed from embryonic signals, frog skin cells form self-motile Xenobots
claim: Frog (Xenopus) embryonic epithelial cells, which in vivo form a passive protective outer layer, instead form Xenobots (functional, self-motile constructs with novel behaviours) when liberated from the instructive influences of other cells, showing that such behaviours are normally suppressed by signalling from neighbouring cells during development.
quote: However, when liberated from the instructive influences of the other cells, frog epithelial cells instead form a Xenobot—a functional, self-motile construct with many novel behaviors that are normally suppressed and hidden by the instructive signaling of other cells during development [125].
scope: Xenopus laevis embryonic ectoderm explants
measurable_quantities: motility of explants
behavioural repertoire of explants vs in-vivo epidermis
candidate_data: Published Xenobot imaging and behaviour data deposited with the original papers; Xenbase expression data for epidermal cells.

label: Bioelectric networks were exploited for information integration since bacterial biofilms
claim: Evolution discovered very early, around the time of bacterial biofilms, that electrical networks of ion channels and pumps are a convenient way to integrate and process information across space and time and to scale the functions of individual cells toward large-scale tasks, the same reason brains use this modality.
quote: But evolution discovered very early on, around the time of bacterial biofilms [144], that electric networks are also extremely convenient ways to integrate and process information across space and time, and to scale the functions of individual computing units towards a large-scale task (the same reason that brains, and computers, use this modality [145]).
scope: Bacteria through metazoans
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distribution of ion channel families
presence of electrical signalling in biofilms and non-neural tissues
candidate_data: Ion channel family phylogenies from Pfam/InterPro and UniProt; published biofilm electrophysiology data.

label: Reproducing face bioelectric patterns via ion-channel misexpression induces ectopic eyes
claim: The vertebrate face is patterned by bioelectric gradients that regionalize gene expression, and reproducing these voltage patterns elsewhere in a tadpole by misexpressing specific ion channels induces whole ectopic organs such as eyes on the gut or tail, regions not otherwise competent to make eyes in response to Pax6.
quote: Reproducing these patterns elsewhere in the body via misexpression of specific ion channels enables the induction of whole ectopic organs, such as eyes [152] on the gut or tail of a tadpole (thus unlocking novel capabilities of body regions, since only the anterior neurectoderm is competent to make eyes via signals from the chemical master regulator Pax6).
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos and tadpoles
measurable_quantities: resting membrane potential of injected regions
incidence and location of ectopic eyes
candidate_data: Published Xenopus voltage-dye imaging and ectopic-eye incidence data; Xenbase for ion channel and eye-field gene expression.

label: Tadpoles see through an ectopic tail eye without generations of adaptation
claim: Tadpoles whose native eyes are prevented from forming and which carry an ectopic eye on the tail can see and perform well in visual behavioural training even though that eye connects to the spinal cord or peripheral tissue rather than the brain, so a radical change to sensory–motor architecture yields successful behaviour without generations of adaptation.
quote: Tadpoles, in which the native eyes are prevented from forming and an ectopic eye is instead placed on the tail, can see and perform well in visual behavioral training [176], even though the ectopic eye connects to the spinal cord (or just to peripheral tissue) rather than to the brain—this radical change to the sensory–motor architecture does not require generations of adaptation to produce successful behavior.
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with ectopic eye grafts
measurable_quantities: visual learning performance of eyeless tadpoles with tail eyes
axon projection targets of ectopic eyes
candidate_data: Published Xenopus ectopic-eye behavioural training data; Xenbase anatomy resources.

label: Polyploid newt kidney tubules are built by one giant cell instead of eight to ten
claim: In polyploid newts, whose cells are enlarged by extra genome copies, kidney tubules normally made by eight to ten communicating cells are instead formed by a single enormous cell wrapping around itself, so a different molecular mechanism (cytoskeletal bending rather than cell–cell communication) is deployed to reach the same anatomical outcome, an instance of downward causation in the service of a large-scale anatomical goal.
quote: In the kidney system of polyploid newts, the normal cell:cell communication that creates a tubule from eight to ten cells working together is swapped for a single enormous cell that wraps around itself to create the same final outcome [184].
scope: Polyploid newt pronephric/kidney tubules
measurable_quantities: cells per tubule cross-section by ploidy
tubule diameter by ploidy
cell size
candidate_data: Classic histological data on polyploid newts in the cited literature; new histology on induced polyploid amphibians.

label: Bioelectric patterns act as hidden layers that split the genotype–anatomy inverse problem
claim: Bioelectric networks mitigate the inverse problem of morphogenesis by acting as 'hidden layers' between genetics and anatomy: the mapping from ion channel genes to bioelectric pattern, and from bioelectric pattern to anatomy, are each easier to invert than the direct genotype–anatomy map, decomposing the control problem into two easier ones for evolution and for engineers.
quote: The relationships of ion channel genes to the bioelectric pattern, and bioelectric pattern to its resulting anatomy, are each easier to invert than the direct genotype–anatomy link, so they help to decompose the control problem into two easier problems.
scope: Bioelectric control of morphogenesis in animals
measurable_quantities: predictability of anatomy from bioelectric pattern vs from genotype
predictability of bioelectric pattern from ion channel expression
candidate_data: Paired ion-channel expression (e.g. Gene Expression Omnibus) and voltage-imaging datasets with anatomical outcomes; computational bioelectric models such as those in BioModels.

label: Voltage is the instructive variable: an unrelated yeast pump can replace tail V-ATPase
claim: Membrane voltage is a coarse-grained, high-order parameter over ion channel and pump microstates: electrogenic proteins can be swapped as long as the bioelectric state is correct, e.g. the V-ATPase function in tadpole tail regeneration can be phenocopied by a yeast proton pump with no sequence or structural homology.
quote: electrogenic proteins can be swapped out as needed (e.g., V-ATPase complex in the tadpole tail can be phenocopied by a yeast proton pump with no sequence or structural homology, because it produces the correct physiological signal), and everything still works as long as the bioelectric state is correct [190].
scope: Xenopus tadpole tail regeneration; bioelectric control generally
measurable_quantities: tail regeneration rate under V-ATPase inhibition with and without heterologous pump
membrane potential of regenerating tissue
candidate_data: Published Xenopus tail-regeneration rescue data; Xenbase expression data for V-ATPase subunits.

label: Genetically wild-type planarian cells can store more than one target morphology
claim: In planaria, a brief (2-day) physiological intervention can reset the bioelectric circuit that controls head number from the default one-head pattern memory to a two-head pattern, so the same genetically wild-type cells can harbour multiple bioelectrically encoded target morphologies that guide regeneration.
quote: In this case, the exact same hardware (genetically wild-type planarian cells) can harbor multiple representations of the bioelectrically encoded target morphology that guides the cellular collectives during regeneration [193–195].
scope: Planarians (Dugesia japonica and related species) during regeneration
measurable_quantities: head number after amputation following transient bioelectric perturbation
persistence of altered phenotype across rounds of amputation
candidate_data: Published planarian two-head regeneration data; PlanMine and SmedGD for planarian gene and transcriptome resources.

label: Bioelectric changes let wild-type planaria grow other species' head shapes in days
claim: Head shapes of existing planarian species are readily recapitulated by genetically wild-type planaria whose bioelectric circuit is altered during regeneration, so 100–150 million years of evolutionary distance in morphospace can be crossed in a few days through the dynamics of bioelectric pattern memories.
quote: Indeed, it has been shown that existing planarian species’ head shapes are readily recapitulated by a genetically wild-type animal experiencing changes to its bioelectric circuit during regeneration—100–150 million years of evolutionary distance in morphospace can be crossed in a few days because of the dynamics of bioelectric pattern memories [197, 198].
scope: Planarians (e.g. Girardia dorotocephala) treated with gap-junction blockers during regeneration
measurable_quantities: head shape morphometrics of treated vs other species
divergence times between planarian species
candidate_data: Published planarian head morphometrics; planarian molecular phylogenies and divergence estimates (e.g. TimeTree); PlanMine.

label: Surgically altered ciliate cortex is inherited across generations despite wild-type DNA
claim: In unicellular ciliates, changes made to cell-surface form can be inherited across generations independently of DNA: surgical rotation of a small patch of cortex creates a stable line in which part of the ciliary beat pushes food out of the mouth, which the wild-type genome cannot correct.
quote: Changes made to unicellular form can persist across generations [203–205]; for example, surgical rotation of a small patch of the cell surface creates a stable line of animals in which a portion of the ciliary beat pushes food out of their mouths—a condition which their perfectly wild-type genome cannot correct.
scope: Ciliates such as Paramecium and Tetrahymena
measurable_quantities: inheritance of inverted ciliary rows over generations
feeding efficiency of altered lines
candidate_data: Classic cortical-inheritance studies; ParameciumDB and the Tetrahymena Genome Database for genetic background.

label: Planaria adapt to barium by changing expression of only a handful of genes
claim: Planaria exposed to barium, a non-specific potassium channel blocker that is evolutionarily novel to them, first lose their heads but then regrow barium-insensitive heads, with only a handful of genes up- or down-regulated, showing that cells can navigate transcriptional space to solve a problem for which there was no selection.
quote: Transcriptional analysis reveals that these tissues up- and down-regulate just a handful of genes to get back to physiological and anatomical setpoints despite the inability to regulate potassium.
scope: Planarians cultured in barium chloride
measurable_quantities: number of differentially expressed genes in barium-adapted heads
head degeneration and regrowth time
candidate_data: The cited barium-adaptation transcriptome, if deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus; PlanMine and SmedGD.

label: Animals with robust regeneration also resist cancer and aging
claim: Animals with robust morphogenetic control due to high plasticity are resistant to perturbation at many scales: they regenerate lost limbs and organs, readily suppress cancer, and resist aging, contrary to the expectation that easy access to undifferentiated cells should make them highly cancer-prone.
quote: Animals with robust morphogenetic control due to high levels of plasticity are resistant to changes of circumstance (injury) at many scales: they regenerate after loss of limbs and organs (degradation of body-scale information), they suppress cancer readily [238] (degradation of tissue-scale information) and they resist aging (degradation of cell-level information).
scope: Animals across taxa, especially highly regenerative ones such as planaria and salamanders
measurable_quantities: regenerative capacity
cancer incidence
lifespan or ageing rate across species
candidate_data: AnAge lifespan data; comparative cancer-incidence data from zoo necropsies; published regeneration-capacity surveys.

label: Competency gains drive a ratchet toward ever greater multiscale competency
claim: Because each gain in developmental competency makes the structural genome harder for selection to evaluate, evolution increasingly optimizes the competency mechanisms themselves, a feedback ratchet for multiscale intelligence that appears in computational models and has run to different extents in planaria, salamanders and mammals.
quote: This starts a feedback loop, because each gain in competency makes it even harder to judge the structural genome, which exacerbates the drive toward improving competencies—a ratchet for multiscale intelligence that can readily be seen in computational models of the process [240].
scope: Evolution of metazoans; computational models of evolving competent cells
measurable_quantities: competency level over generations in evolutionary simulations
genome messiness vs anatomical robustness across lineages
candidate_data: Published simulations of competency evolution; comparative genomics of planaria and other regenerators (PlanMine).

label: The competency ratchet predicts no planarian mutant strains with abnormal morphology
claim: The competency-ratchet model predicts, and it is the case, that there are no known mutant planarian strains with abnormal morphologies (unlike flies or mice), explains the difficulty of making transgenic planaria, and the only known permanent abnormal planarian lines (two-headed and randomized 1- vs 2-head forms) arose from bioelectric rather than genetic change.
quote: For example, it predicts the confirmed fact that there are no known mutant planarian strains with abnormal morphologies (the way there are for fruit flies, mice, etc.) and explains why the research community has had such a hard time (despite decades of efforts) generating transgenic planaria.
scope: Planarians compared with Drosophila, mice and other model organisms
measurable_quantities: number of heritable morphological mutant strains per model organism
success rate of planarian transgenesis
candidate_data: Strain catalogues such as FlyBase and MGI for comparison; planarian community resources (SmedGD, PlanMine) and published transgenesis attempts.

label: Multiscale competency smooths the fitness landscape and lets search escape local maxima
claim: The multiscale competency architecture smooths the fitness landscape by reducing phenotypic differences between genotypes, letting evolution explore mutations that would otherwise be lethal (e.g. a mutation that displaces the mouth but has another benefit survives because the mouth self-corrects), which makes search more efficient and helps it overcome local maxima.
quote: By smoothing the fitness landscape, MCA makes the search process much more efficient, improving evolvability by enabling the search to overcome local maxima.
scope: Evolution of organisms with regulative development
measurable_quantities: fitness-landscape ruggedness with vs without developmental error correction
evolvability in simulations
candidate_data: Evolutionary simulations with developmental error-correction; Xenopus craniofacial remodelling data from the cited studies.

label: Developmental error-correction makes mutations neutral and builds up cryptic variation
claim: By buffering mutational effects through developmental regulation, the multiscale competency architecture makes neutral many mutations that would be deleterious under a direct genotype-to-phenotype mapping, so they persist as a pool of phenotypically dormant cryptic variation that can later be exploited.
quote: MCA makes many mutations neutral that would be deleterious in a direct genotype → phenotype architecture. Such mutations whose effects are mitigated by developmental regulation are not weeded out; instead, they persist, generating over time a rich pool of diversity that may be phenotypically dormant, but can be exploited in future.
scope: Evolving populations of organisms with regulative development
measurable_quantities: standing cryptic genetic variation
phenotypic variance released when buffering is disrupted
candidate_data: Cryptic-variation release experiments (e.g. Hsp90 inhibition studies); population genomic data such as the Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel.

label: A collective's perceptual field and ability to find alternative paths grow with its size
claim: Extending William James' definition of intelligence (reaching the same goal by different means) to collectives via the perceptual field, the region of space and time an agent can survey for alternative paths to a goal, the authors propose that as a collective grows its perceptual field increases, improving its ability to find variant paths.
quote: As the size of a collective increases its perceptual field increases, improving its ability to find variant paths.
scope: Cell collectives and other biological collectives
measurable_quantities: spatial and temporal range of signals integrated by a collective
rate of successful re-routing after perturbation vs collective size
candidate_data: Collective cell migration imaging datasets (e.g. in the Cell Image Library) varying group size.

label: Neural unification into a self is a pivot of earlier morphogenetic cell communication
claim: It has been hypothesized, and the authors adopt, that the ability of neurons to unify into a centralized self is an evolutionary pivot of earlier cell-communication strategies that first solved problems in anatomical morphospace, a domain also requiring information processing above the single-cell level.
quote: Indeed it has been hypothesized that the remarkable ability of neurons to unify toward a centralized self – the emergent agent that is the subject of memories, preferences, and goals which are not assignable to any of the individual components – is an evolutionary pivot of far earlier cell communication strategies that first solved problems in navigating another domain that requires information processing above the single cell level: anatomical morphospace70.
scope: Evolution of nervous systems from non-neural bioelectric signalling in metazoans
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic distribution of neural signalling molecules in non-neural developmental roles
candidate_data: Comparative genomics of ion channels and neurotransmitter pathways in early-branching metazoans (e.g. sponge and placozoan genomes in Ensembl Metazoa).

label: The number of embryos a blastoderm forms is not fixed by genetics
claim: The number of individuals formed by an embryonic blastoderm is not fixed at one by the genome: temporarily introducing breaks that informationally isolate islands of cells yields twins, triplets and so on, showing the blastoderm is an excitable medium in which several coherent embryos can self-organize.
quote: Indeed, the question of how many individuals are present in an embryonic blastoderm is not fixed at 1 by the genetics, because temporary introduction of breaks in the blastoderm (leading to informational isolation of islands of cell masses) results in twins, triplets, etc103.
scope: Early vertebrate (e.g. avian) blastoderms
measurable_quantities: number of embryonic axes formed after blastoderm cuts
cut geometry
candidate_data: Classic chick blastoderm cutting experiments in the cited literature; new embryo-splitting experiments.

label: Keratocyte fragments migrate to the anode while whole keratocytes migrate to the cathode
claim: In an electric field, whole keratocytes migrate toward the cathode while fragments of keratocytes migrate toward the anode, so the collective (an intact cell) has the opposite taxis to its parts, illustrating that collective behaviour can be a hard-to-predict function of component tendencies.
quote: In an electric field, keratocytes migrate to the cathode, but fragments of keratocytes migrate to the anode104.
scope: Fish keratocytes and keratocyte fragments in applied electric fields
measurable_quantities: galvanotaxis direction of whole cells vs fragments
migration speed
candidate_data: Published keratocyte galvanotaxis time-lapse data; Cell Image Library.

label: Targeting instructor-cell voltage converts tadpole melanocytes to a melanoma-like state
claim: In Xenopus tadpoles, briefly targeting the bioelectric state of a small population of instructor cells (with a chloride channel activator or a GlyCl mutant), in the absence of carcinogens, oncogenes or DNA damage, converts melanocytes throughout the animal, including distant ones, into an over-proliferative, invasive melanoma-like phenotype via disruption of serotonergic signalling.
quote: This could be achieved in the absence of classical carcinogens, oncogenes, or DNA damage, by brief exposure to chemical (chloride ion channel activator drug) or molecular-genetic (GlyCl mutant) targeting of the bioelectric state of a specific cell population: instructor cells which normally keep the melanocytes in their healthy state via serotonergic signaling118.
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles
measurable_quantities: membrane potential of instructor cells
melanocyte number, shape and invasiveness
serotonin signalling levels
candidate_data: Published Xenopus hyperpigmentation datasets from the cited studies; Xenbase for glycine receptor and melanocyte markers.

label: Melanocyte conversion is all-or-none per animal, stochastic only across the cohort
claim: Melanocyte conversion after instructor-cell depolarization is a collective, all-or-none decision: different reagents give different incidences in a cohort (e.g. 70% converted), but each animal is either fully converted or fully normal; a computational model fitted to these incidences predicted interventions (two drugs and a dominant-negative construct) that were then confirmed to produce the first partially converted animals.
quote: Using different reagents could induce different incidences of hyperpigmentation (conversion) in a cohort of animals, but this was a population-level phenotype: for example, 70% of the animals could be converted, but any given animal was either fully converted or fully normal (Fig. 4a, b).
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with perturbed instructor-cell bioelectric signalling
measurable_quantities: fraction of animals converted
fraction of melanocytes converted within each animal
candidate_data: Published per-animal hyperpigmentation scoring from the cited studies and the associated model.

label: Head-versus-tail choice at a planarian cut cannot be made locally
claim: When a planarian is cut once, cells that were adjacent neighbours at the same positional-information value make a head on one side and a tail on the other, so this anatomical decision cannot be made locally: wound cells must coordinate with the rest of the fragment to learn where they are, which way they face and what structures remain.
quote: In other words, it is actually impossible for an anatomical decision like this to be made locally – the cells of the wound must coordinate with the remaining fragment to get information about where they are located, which way they are facing, and what other structures exist121,122, in order to make adaptive decisions about large-scale growth and form that enable regeneration of normal worms.
scope: Regenerating planarian fragments
measurable_quantities: head/tail fate at each wound
long-range signalling (bioelectric, gap-junctional) between wound and fragment
candidate_data: Planarian regeneration studies with gap-junction knockdown; PlanMine and SmedGD.

label: Cryptic planaria randomize head number per animal, not per cell
claim: Perturbing the planarian bioelectric control circuit produces 'Cryptic' destabilized worms whose fragments, even from the same parent, regenerate one-headed and two-headed forms at a set frequency of about 1:2, yet each animal has clear heads and tails rather than mixed tissue, so the randomized bioelectric state is interpreted by collectives rather than by individual cells.
quote: More specifically, several perturbations targeting the bioelectric control circuit (Fig. 5e) have shown randomization of outcome: such Cryptic planaria are destabilized, and fragments (even from the same parent worm) will form 1-head and 2-head forms at a set frequency of ~1:2130 (Fig. 5f).
scope: Planarians after gap-junction or bioelectric perturbation
measurable_quantities: ratio of 1-head to 2-head regenerates
spatial homogeneity of head/tail marker expression within each worm
candidate_data: Published Cryptic planaria regeneration counts; PlanMine.

label: Left-right randomization is concordant within an embryo except after VANGL knockdown
claim: Bioelectric and biochemical perturbations of vertebrate left-right patterning randomize laterality only at the level of whole embryos (each embryo's cells agree on L and R identity); the only known perturbation that breaks this concordance is down-regulation of planar-polarity VANGL signalling, which produces speckled L/R marker expression on both sides of the midline.
quote: In all of the many studies on perturbation of the LR pathway, we are aware of only one that actually breaks the concordance: disruption of the planar polarity pathway by down-regulating VANGL signaling149 leads to a speckling on both sides of the midline, consistent with individual cells within a single lateral domain disagreeing on whether they should have L or R identity (Fig. 6a–d).
scope: Vertebrate embryos (chick, Xenopus and others) with perturbed left-right pathways
measurable_quantities: laterality marker (e.g. Pitx2, Nodal) expression per embryo and per cell
incidence of heterotaxy and isomerism
candidate_data: Published left-right perturbation studies; Xenbase and ZFIN laterality-marker expression data.

label: Grafted groups of neural crest cells keep their identity; single grafted cells do not
claim: Single neural crest cells transposed to a different anterior-posterior axial domain change their gene expression to match their neighbours, whereas groups of transposed cells keep their original gene expression, which the authors interpret as collectives having greater positional memory (a perceptual field extending further into the past) than individual cells.
quote: Individual cells transposed from one anterior-posterior axial domain to another will change their gene expression to match their neighbors159,161,162. In contrast, groups of cells transposed along the anterior-posterior axis maintain their original gene expression, thus resisting the inductive effects of the surrounding tissue159,161,162.
scope: Vertebrate neural crest (chick, mouse) transplantation
measurable_quantities: Hox gene expression of grafted cells vs graft size
time to lose original identity
candidate_data: Published neural crest transplantation studies; single-cell RNA-seq of neural crest in the Gene Expression Omnibus.

label: The segmentation clock needs a cell collective to oscillate and entrains grafted cells
claim: The vertebrate segmentation clock depends on collectivity: presomitic mesoderm cells do not oscillate when cultured individually but resume oscillating when cultured together, wild-type cells grafted into non-cycling mutant fish express her1 without cycling, and cells grafted into tissue at a different clock phase synchronize to their neighbours' phase.
quote: Similarly, pre-somitic mesoderm cells do not oscillate when cultured independently, but will resume oscillating when cultured collectively169.
scope: Vertebrate presomitic mesoderm (zebrafish, chick, mouse)
measurable_quantities: oscillation of clock reporters in isolated vs aggregated cells
phase of grafted cells over time
candidate_data: Published segmentation-clock live-imaging datasets; ZFIN for her1 expression and mutants.

label: Frog embryo brain gene expression is driven by voltage differences, not absolute values
claim: In the frog embryo brain, downstream gene expression is driven by the spatial difference in membrane voltage between regions rather than the absolute voltage of any cells, so cells must read patterns over whole cell fields: collectivity appears in the input as well as the output of cell-group behaviour.
quote: For example, in the frog embryo brain, it is the spatial difference in voltage between regions that drives downstream gene expression, not the absolute value of any cells186,187.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryonic brain patterning
measurable_quantities: regional resting membrane potentials
brain patterning gene expression under uniform vs differential voltage shifts
candidate_data: Published Xenopus voltage-dye and brain-marker data from the cited studies; Xenbase.
